newsitem.title: HONG KONG: CRICKET - CRICKETERS TRY TO BOWL CHINESE OVER IN HONG KONG.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET - CRICKETERS TRY TO BOWL CHINESE OVER IN HONG KONG.

text.p: There is a corner of a foreign field which is forever England -- if the Hong Kong Cricket Association has anything to do with it.
The sun is setting on Britain's empire in Hong Kong with the handover to China on June 30, but the quintessentially English game of cricket is set to live on.
Hong Kong's cricket heroes of tomorrow will even be joining in the handover celebrations -- kitted out in red shirts, white trousers and Hong Kong cricket club caps for a big sports parade on July 3.
And the Hong Kong Cricket Association believes China's new Special Administrative Region could be a launching pad to attract another one billion potential cricket devotees.
The perennial problem in Hong Kong, one of the most crowded and frenetic places on earth, is finding enough space to play cricket.
The Association has set up six cricket centres where 450 Chinese children have enrolled.
"Kids living on the 30th floor don't have much space and like children everywhere they love to whack around a ball," said association executive director Russell Mawhinney.
"Finding grounds is a difficult problem. We are tightly squashed in here," he said.

The New Zealander eagerly promotes cricket to the Chinese: "It is a non-contact sport that takes plenty of grey matter. We think we have advantages over other sports. It can be played by all shapes and sizes," he said.

Hong Kong also has 50 adult cricket teams but the association is keen to develop the sport among young Chinese so that it does not have an elitist image as a genteel and obscure game for expatriates only.
"Twenty-two gweilos (Westerners) running around a field won't get much sympathy," Mawhinney told Reuters in an interview.
So the Association has been going with bat, ball and instruction video in hand to explain the intricacies and attractions of the game to the authorities in the new Hong Kong.
"It is pretty basic stuff, what it is, how you play it. Some take a negative stance but most are overwhelmingly supportive," Mawhinney said.
"Hong Kong could be a pilot model to take into China but it is going to take a big cash injection. The International Cricket Council is on the case," he said.
Seeing China on the international cricket stage may be a pipe dream at the moment but Mawhinney said: "It is not incoceivable in 15-20 years."

But what of the expatriates sailing off into the sunset as 156 years of colonial rule end in Hong Kong? Would they rather that the game -- as English as a cup of tea or a bowler hat -- should die with them?

"There is a certain amount of ambivalence on the part of some expats who will be leaving anyway," Mawhinney said. "But it is best to focus on the kids. This is something to be proud of and it will ensure the survival of the game."
